section_summary: This section documents a wave of protests from pottery manufacturers, trade representatives, mayors, and members of Congress against a State Department effort to recruit two American ceramic engineers for the military government in occupied Japan. Critics feared that taxpayer-funded technical assistance would revive low-cost Japanese ceramic exports and damage American pottery employment, while several suggested that Japan instead be required to adopt American-style wage, hour, and social-security standards. State Department replies consistently explained that the War Department would have employed and paid the engineers and that General Douglas MacArthur had withdrawn the request.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on pottery-industry protests and unanswered correspondence
subfiles.about: Hanson reports that five letters protest the proposed recruitment of American ceramic engineers for service in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says General MacArthur requested two American ceramic engineers to work with the military government in Japan, provoking protests from the United States pottery industry. Hanson reports that recruitment officer T. M. Brewer said MacArthur had withdrawn the request and notes that several congressmen wanted help answering constituent letters. He asks that the scattered and previously unanswered protests be handled promptly.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum requesting review of a draft reply
subfiles.about: Hanson asks Mr. Martin to revise a proposed reply concerning the ceramic-engineer controversy.
subfiles.summary: Hanson says the matter was referred to Assistant Secretary Benton by the House Small Business Committee, with which the Department had been cooperating. He prepared a draft using information from Martin and Whitman and stresses the need to send a prompt answer that could be shared with the committee.

subfiles.title: Handwritten policy notes on the proposed ceramic advisers
subfiles.about: The notes outline factual and policy points for answering objections to the proposed ceramic-engineer appointments.
subfiles.summary: The notes state that the request originated with MacArthur, that the engineers' precise work had not been fully explained, and that the State Department was merely servicing a War Department recruitment request. They connect the proposal with occupation policy aimed at a peaceful, self-supporting Japan and reducing the American cost of occupation. They also note the absence of guarantees about Japanese exports, uncertainty about the intended markets, and a need for informal interagency review of similar cases.

subfiles.title: Reply to J. M. Wells announcing withdrawal of the request
subfiles.about: The Department answers Wells's April 1 protest by stating that General MacArthur withdrew the request for two ceramic engineers.
subfiles.summary: The letter clarifies that the military authorities requested the engineers and that the War Department, rather than the State Department, would have employed and paid them. It then reports that General MacArthur withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: Recruitment request for two ceramic engineers
subfiles.about: Brewer requests assistance identifying two ceramic engineers to advise the military government's economic and scientific section in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter seeks highly qualified technicians with broad ceramic experience for positions paying up to $7,800 per year. It explains that the War Department controlled the appointments while the State Department recruited specialized personnel under a cooperative arrangement. Brewer also describes the minimum nine-month term, government transportation, inexpensive Army quarters and meals, and restrictions on accompanying families.

subfiles.title: J. M. Wells protest against assistance to Japanese potters
subfiles.about: Wells angrily rejects Brewer's request and argues that American assistance would strengthen Japanese competition at the expense of domestic pottery workers.
subfiles.summary: Wells characterizes the proposal as a taxpayer-funded effort to take jobs from Americans who had fought Japan. He disputes free-trade arguments by contrasting the high American wage content of displaced china production with the lower wage content of compensating exports. Citing prewar import statistics, he says Japan already possessed advanced ceramic skills and asks that any government-supported technical work benefit American potters instead.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on congressional and municipal protests
subfiles.about: MacKnight reports Brewer's conversation with Congressman Noble J. Johnson and calls for an answer to Minerva's mayor.
subfiles.summary: Brewer told MacKnight that Congressman Noble J. Johnson had received several protest letters and wanted copies of the Department's outgoing correspondence. MacKnight promised him a copy of the reply to Wells and reminded Hanson that the mayor of Minerva had also written in protest. A fragmentary handwritten note on page 10 appears related to Brewer's request.

subfiles.title: Mayor W. Ray Brown's protest to T. M. Brewer
subfiles.about: Minerva's mayor protests recruiting American engineers to assist the Japanese ceramic industry.
subfiles.summary: Brown cites claims that Japan supplied more than eighty percent of American china dinnerware before the war, while American factories supplied only about three percent. He argues that using pottery workers' taxes to strengthen a low-cost foreign competitor would cause unemployment in American ceramic communities. He urges the Department to reconsider the proposal.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mayor W. Ray Brown
subfiles.about: The Department informs Mayor Brown that MacArthur withdrew the ceramic-engineer request.
subfiles.summary: The letter answers Brown's April 22 protest concerning advisers for the Japanese ceramic industry. It states that General MacArthur withdrew his request for the two engineers.

subfiles.title: Mayor W. Ray Brown's protest to Secretary Byrnes
subfiles.about: Brown sends Secretary Byrnes a version of his protest against technical aid to Japanese ceramics.
subfiles.summary: Brown argues that Japan already dominated the prewar American dinnerware market and could sell high-quality products at prices domestic manufacturers could not match. He objects to spending American tax money on Japanese industry and predicts that renewed imports would cost American ceramic workers their jobs. The text substantially duplicates his letter to Brewer.

subfiles.title: Reply to Royal Hickman
subfiles.about: Acheson explains the departmental responsibility for the proposed engineers and announces withdrawal of the request.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that the military authorities in Japan requested the two engineers and that the War Department would employ and pay them. It reports that General MacArthur subsequently withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: Royal Hickman's protest against promoting Japanese ceramics
subfiles.about: Hickman protests government assistance to Japanese dinnerware and pottery production.
subfiles.summary: Hickman argues that rebuilding Japanese ceramics would recreate severe competition for American potters and would be unlike the protective policies of other governments. Identifying himself as a leading American ceramic designer and manufacturer, he asks that the proposal be abandoned immediately. Copies were directed to chambers of commerce and several Tennessee legislators.

subfiles.title: Ohio Chamber of Commerce request for clarification
subfiles.about: Atkinson asks whether the proposed engineers would supervise and report on Japanese ceramics rather than teach improved production methods.
subfiles.summary: The Ohio Chamber had received vigorous objections to Brewer's March 19 recruitment letter. Atkinson suggests that the engineers' proper task might be to study and supervise Japanese activity for the American government, not improve a competing industry. He asks for information that he can relay to ceramic interests in and near Ohio.

subfiles.title: Reply to Herschel C. Atkinson
subfiles.about: The Department tells Atkinson that MacArthur withdrew the request for two engineers.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Atkinson's April 25 inquiry. It says the military government requested the engineers, the War Department would employ and pay them, and General MacArthur withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: John Frier's protest and labor-standards proposal
subfiles.about: Frier condemns technical aid to Japanese pottery and proposes raising Japanese labor and welfare standards instead.
subfiles.summary: Frier says his small manufacturing business suffered before the war because Japanese workers' low wages allowed manufacturers to undersell American producers. Rather than sending pottery experts, he recommends establishing a living minimum wage, a forty-hour week with overtime premiums, Social Security, pensions, and support for dependent children in Japan. He argues that such reforms would help Japanese workers while reducing unfair competition.

subfiles.title: Reply to John Frier
subfiles.about: The Department advises Frier that MacArthur withdrew the request for ceramic engineers.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges Frier's April 27 protest. It clarifies that the military authorities requested the engineers and the War Department would employ and pay them, then announces the request's withdrawal.

subfiles.title: Senator Homer Ferguson forwards Frank H. Riddle's complaint
subfiles.about: Ferguson forwards a constituent letter and newspaper clipping about the recruitment controversy and requests an explanation.
subfiles.summary: The enclosures concern correspondence between J. M. Wells and T. M. Brewer over two ceramic advisers for Japan. Ferguson explains that Frank H. Riddle fears renewed Japanese competition in tableware sold in the United States. He asks for the enclosures to be returned with information he can use in replying.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Homer Ferguson
subfiles.about: The Department returns Ferguson's enclosures and answers his inquiry about the ceramic advisers.
subfiles.summary: The reply returns the material Ferguson sent concerning recruitment for Japan. As in related responses, it explains the military origin and War Department financing of the request and reports its withdrawal.

subfiles.title: William R. Thom forwards the Minerva mayor's protest
subfiles.about: Thom forwards Mayor Brown's protest and asks the Secretary of State for comment.
subfiles.summary: Thom says Minerva is a pottery town whose mayor believes Japanese competition could ruin its chief industry. He encloses a copy of Brown's letter and asks what explanation the Department can provide.

subfiles.title: Copy of Mayor Brown's letter to William R. Thom
subfiles.about: Brown asks Congressman Thom to help block the proposed recruitment of ceramic engineers for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Brown repeats figures claiming that Japanese dinnerware dominated the prewar American market. He argues that American taxpayers should not finance improvements that would make Japanese products even more competitive and cost domestic ceramic workers their jobs. He expressly requests Thom's support in blocking the measure.

subfiles.title: Louis Ludlow forwards an Indiana pottery complaint
subfiles.about: Ludlow transmits a complaint from an Evansville pottery company about sending ceramic experts to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The quoted manufacturer says prewar Japanese dinnerware imports forced curtailed production and destructive price competition in the United States. It also complains that wartime price controls caused the company to operate at a loss and warns that Japan would soon become a serious competitor again. Ludlow asks Brewer to consider these views and advise him.

subfiles.title: Reply to Louis Ludlow
subfiles.about: Byrnes informs Ludlow that MacArthur withdrew the request for the two engineers.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Ludlow's April 30 letter to Brewer. It says the military government requested the engineers, the War Department would employ and pay them, and General MacArthur withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: Reply to William R. Thom
subfiles.about: Acheson answers Thom's inquiry by reporting withdrawal of the ceramic-engineer request.
subfiles.summary: The letter clarifies that the engineers had been requested by the military authorities and would have been employed and paid by the War Department. It states that General MacArthur withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: Margaret S. Schmidt's protest against Japanese ceramic rehabilitation
subfiles.about: Schmidt opposes having American manufacturers assist the revival of low-priced Japanese china production.
subfiles.summary: Writing as a representative of a ceramic-art line, Schmidt recalls the hardship caused by low-priced Japanese imports. She accepts that Japan must produce goods to live but argues that its output should be directed to nearby Asian markets and Russia rather than compete in the United States. She closes by saying that Americans feeding the world should at least make the plates on which the food is served.

subfiles.title: Reply to Margaret S. Schmidt
subfiles.about: Russell informs Schmidt that General MacArthur withdrew the request for the ceramic engineers.
subfiles.summary: The response acknowledges Schmidt's May 1 letter. It explains that the military government requested the engineers and the War Department would employ and pay them, but the request had now been withdrawn.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Homer E. Capehart
subfiles.about: Byrnes answers Capehart's protest by reporting the withdrawal of the engineer request.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges Capehart's May 6 communication to Brewer. It repeats that the military authorities requested the engineers, the War Department would employ and pay them, and MacArthur withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: Senator Homer E. Capehart's protest
subfiles.about: Capehart protests using American tax money to provide ceramic technical advice in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Capehart says sending engineers to teach Japanese ceramic producers would place them in direct competition with the American pottery industry. He emphasizes Japan's low wage standards and urges the Department to reconsider. He asks to be informed of the final decision.

subfiles.title: Charles A. Halleck inquiry about ceramic advisers
subfiles.about: Halleck asks what the Department intends to do about reports of sending ceramic engineers to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Halleck says he has received protests alleging that government-funded American engineers would teach the Japanese to improve and expand ceramic production. He asks the Department to explain what action is actually contemplated.

subfiles.title: Reply to Charles A. Halleck
subfiles.about: Acheson tells Halleck that MacArthur withdrew the request for the ceramic engineers.
subfiles.summary: The reply says the military government in Japan requested the engineers and the War Department would employ and pay them. It reports that General MacArthur withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: Reply to Frank A. Mathews Jr.
subfiles.about: Acheson answers Mathews's protest by announcing withdrawal of the ceramic-engineer request.
subfiles.summary: The response identifies the military authorities in Japan as the source of the request and the War Department as the intended employer and paymaster. It then states that General MacArthur withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: Frank A. Mathews Jr.'s protest
subfiles.about: Mathews vigorously protests reports that American engineers would help Japan compete with pottery plants in his district.
subfiles.summary: Mathews says his New Jersey district contains major ceramic and pottery plants and argues that they should not be taxed to develop a former enemy into a competitor. He contrasts American living standards with Japan's low standards and compares the proposal to prewar exports of oil and scrap iron to Japan. He asks Byrnes for an explanation and registers an emphatic protest.

subfiles.title: Senator Joseph F. Guffey forwards industry correspondence
subfiles.about: Guffey forwards complaints from M. E. K. Hommel and the United States Potters Association and requests comments.
subfiles.summary: Guffey assumes the Department has received many protests concerning the same ceramic-engineer proposal. He asks that the enclosed letters and supporting material be returned with comments he can use in answering the correspondents.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Joseph F. Guffey
subfiles.about: Byrnes reports withdrawal of the request and returns Guffey's correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The reply says the military government requested the ceramic engineers and the War Department would employ and pay them. Byrnes states that General MacArthur withdrew the request and returns four enclosed letters dated March 19, April 1, and April 30.

subfiles.title: Reply to A. L. Bulwinkle
subfiles.about: Byrnes advises Bulwinkle that General MacArthur withdrew the request for ceramic engineers.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges Bulwinkle's May 15 protest. It explains that the military government requested the engineers and the War Department would employ and pay them, but MacArthur withdrew the request.

subfiles.title: A. L. Bulwinkle's protest against ceramic assistance
subfiles.about: Bulwinkle argues that Japanese potters need no instruction and that the program would harm American manufacturers and mineral producers.
subfiles.summary: Bulwinkle notes that Japan had long produced fine pottery and that imported Japanese china previously flooded American markets. He warns that renewed competition would damage not only pottery manufacturers but also American feldspar, kaolin, and clay interests. He calls the proposed program both detrimental and wasteful.

subfiles.title: Senator Tom Connally referral slip
subfiles.about: Connally refers constituent correspondence concerning the ceramic-engineer issue to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: The brief Senate form formally sends the correspondence to the Department for consideration. It bears Connally's name and a file reference for the May 16 referral.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Tom Connally
subfiles.about: Byrnes returns Connally's correspondence and reports that MacArthur withdrew the request.
subfiles.summary: The letter states that the military authorities in Japan requested the engineers and the War Department would have employed and paid them. Byrnes reports the withdrawal and returns three letters dated March 19, April 1, and April 30 for Connally's files.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for Connally enclosure
subfiles.about: The slip records the temporary removal or routing of an enclosure associated with the Connally correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The form identifies file 894.65A/5-1646 and marks an enclosure as charged to the A-B office. A handwritten note appears to say that the material was returned or routed to Senator Connally.

subfiles.title: Reply to James G. Fulton
subfiles.about: Byrnes tells Fulton the engineer request was withdrawn and returns Hommel's letter with a copy of the Department's response.
subfiles.summary: The letter explains that the military authorities requested the engineers and the War Department would employ and pay them. Byrnes says MacArthur withdrew the request. He returns M. E. K. Hommel's April 30 letter and encloses a copy of the direct reply to Hommel.

subfiles.title: James G. Fulton forwards the Hommel complaint
subfiles.about: Fulton forwards a letter from The O. Hommel Company and requests a direct departmental answer.
subfiles.summary: Fulton sends the Hommel correspondence to the Department for attention. He asks officials to answer Hommel directly and notify his Pittsburgh congressional office after doing so.

subfiles.title: Brent Spence inquiry about ceramic experts
subfiles.about: Spence forwards material from the United States Potters Association and asks whether ceramic experts were sent to Japan and for what purpose.
subfiles.summary: Spence encloses a letter and supporting documents from W. A. Betz, Secretary-Treasurer of the United States Potters Association. He requests a clear statement on whether the experts had departed for Japan and what work they were intended to perform.

subfiles.title: Reply to Brent Spence
subfiles.about: McCoy informs Spence that MacArthur withdrew the request and that the Department is no longer seeking applicants.
subfiles.summary: The reply says the military government in Japan requested the engineers and the War Department would employ and pay them. Because General MacArthur withdrew the request, the State Department ended recruitment. Betz's letter and enclosures are returned.

subfiles.title: Reply to M. E. K. Hommel
subfiles.about: The Department answers Hommel's protest by explaining the proposal and announcing its withdrawal.
subfiles.summary: The letter says Hommel's April 30 communication to Congressman Fulton was referred to the Department. It explains that the military government requested the engineers and the War Department would employ and pay them. The request was withdrawn, and a copy of the answer was sent to Fulton.
